## The Rain Archive

The Rain Archive occupied the basement of the old waterworks, where the pipes were dry and the ceilings bowed with damp.

Mara’s job was to catalogue sounds the city no longer heard.

She had brass cylinders full of rain striking pavement, hiss through summer leaves, thunder rolling over the river. There was a hail recording so sharp it made listeners flinch. Another captured the soft,persistent tapping of water on an umbrella.

“Rain beginning on a window,” Mara read from a label. “Duration: eleven minutes.”

“Play it sometime,” her colleague said.

“That’s the entire recording.”

“Then you’ll know exactly when it stops.”

Outside, people wore masks against the dust. The streets had roofs joined overhead by transparent panels, and umbrellas were sold mainly as souvenirs, though nobody could explain why anyone would want to carry a reminder of weather they had never known.

Rain had not fallen for eleven years.

In the Archive, it lived on.

One afternoon, while cleaning the oldest shelves, Mara found a cylinder with no label. Its brass was tarnished green, and one end bore a shallow scratch where the recording wire had nearly broken.

She cleaned it carefully and placed it on the listening machine.

Static came through first—a broad, warm hiss, like a sea viewed from a great height. Then a child’s voice.

“Mama, it’s only a little rain.”

A pause.

“Don’t get your hair wet.”

The cylinder clicked. A faint drizzle followed, delicate and irregular, followed by a laugh that Mara felt more than heard.

She listened again.

The voice was small, but the sentence remained perfectly clear. Whoever had made the recording had been close enough to hear every drop.

Mara checked the catalogue. The cylinder was not listed. The machinery’s dates were unreliable, but its oldest records came from the first year of the drought, when the city had still possessed weather and had not yet learned to think of it as a vanished luxury.

She found a pencil mark inside the case:

*First rain, 6:12 p.m.*

The pencil had almost faded.

Mara copied the words onto a new label in black ink. As she did, she remembered rain arriving in the town where she had grown up. Her mother had opened the windows whenever the sky lowered, saying that rain should always be allowed to come inside.

As if it might be frightened by all that glass.

That evening, Mara carried the cylinder upstairs.

The roof of the waterworks overlooked a courtyard of cracked tiles and empty flowerpots. The city beyond it shone under the permanent copper dusk, its covered streets crowded with people hurrying home before the ventilation systems began their nightly cycle.

Mara set the cylinder on a listening machine she had wheeled up from the Archive.

Static filled the courtyard.

Then came the child’s voice.

“Mama, it’s only a little rain.”

People stopped beneath the awnings.

A man removed his dust mask. A shopkeeper leaned out from a doorway, one hand still resting on the half-raised shutter. Children who had learned about rain from recordings gathered around the machine, staring at the brass cylinder as though it contained a sleeping animal.

The laugh returned.

Then the drizzle.

It was only a recording, faint and old. Yet one by one, the people in the courtyard lifted their faces.

The first drop struck the iron awning above them with a bright, silver note.

Then another fell onto the listening machine.

Then another.

The rain did not arrive all at once. It came hesitatingly, as if someone who had forgotten the way had remembered the first step.

Nobody ran for cover.

The rain spread across the dry tiles, darkening the dust, filling the courtyard with the smell of earth. The covered avenues of the city disappeared beneath a thousand small sounds.

And Mara stood there with the new label in her hand, watching the ink run beneath the rain.

The date, at last, was permanent.
